newsitem.title: UK: U.S. jobs data seen capping London stock market.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobs data seen capping London stock market.

text.p: Worries about a strengthening U.S. economy are expected to keep the British stock market cautious and trading subdued in the lead up to next week's key economic U.S. jobs data, market strategists said on Friday.
The Labor Day weekend in the U.S. is likely to further cap activity and stall a pick up in business in London as the traditional August holiday period comes to an end.
Recent data has prompted a reassessment of U.S. economic growth, and renewed fears of a near-term rise in interest rates has seen the FTSE 100 retreat from record highs.
The closely-watched U.S. payroll data due next Friday is seen by many as an important factor in interest rate policy.

The worry that might include a rise in rates has allowed traders, caught out by the 250-point jump in the FTSE 100 in the past six weeks, to push the market lower and reduce their exposure to another spike in share prices.
"I don't think there's any doubt market-makers would like to see the market lower but they're concerned about marking it down too far and running into more buying," said one senior trader.

Concerns about U.S. interest rates were re-ignited on Thursday after an unexpected upward revision in second quarter gross domestic product, pushing the U.S. long bond yield back above seven percent and sending Wall Street skidding.
U.S. July factory orders and Chicago purchasing managers' data on Friday confirmed strength in the U.S. economy.

"Sentiment has been very, very volatile in the past few months. In the last couple of weeks we've seen a revival of the bearish case that U.S. interest rates will have to go up," said Credit Lyonnais Laing market strategist Corey Miller.
"Still, saying that, we feel that it's unlikely ahead of the November election. The inflation outlook is very benign and that'll give the Federal Reserve scope to lay off raising interest rates."

Despite the biggest drop in British shares in over a month on Thursday and a 64-point fall in the Dow, selling has tended to be patchy and confined to profit-taking or to those companies whose results have disappointed.
That trend is likely to be repeated next week with a number of companies due to report. Overall trading activity is likely to remain light with modest volumes again exaggerating price movements.
At current levels, bond markets provide good support for shares but were they to slip they could take equities with them.

"Around these sort of levels the stock market does appear to be quite comfortably valued -- not overly expensive but not overly cheap either," said Miller who has a 3,750 year-end target for the FTSE 100.
Good dividend growth provides another support for share prices but the key may be how fund managers play their cards on their return from holiday.
With the index over 3,900, cash balances relatively high and dividend flows coming through, the question is whether they will start to become more active.
"It's coming to the end of the quarter and fund managers will be coming under pressure from trustees if they've been seen to be out of the market," said another senior trader.
That may lead to a fresh influx of money into the market, helping support current prices.
The payroll data will give many the opportunity to delay that decision, keeping turnover quiet and trading in a narrow range.
